what_it_does:
Two libraries, one per service. Neither sends anything on import; the only command either runs is --dry.

DeepSeek client. Serves stage C's DeepSeek half and stage E's five examiners. (1) Prefix completion, the device W8 part B10 names as the only real test of the port-setting arm: prefix_message() builds the assistant message with prefix true, and the host is chosen from the messages, so a prefix can never go to the standard endpoint where the feature is off. (2) Both sides whole, for PA.1: the client serialises the body itself and posts those bytes, so the saved request text is the text sent; the record carries the body, the exact text, the endpoint, headers with the key redacted, every attempt, the assembled message, finish reason, usage, and the raw SSE lines or the whole JSON. A failure carries the same record out on the exception. (3) Requests and retries kept apart, because PA.1 predicts one request per step in arms (b), (c), (c') and (d) and a retry is a second attempt at the same request, not a second request. (4) Five worker threads at most, W10 section 2's number; six raises with the plan quoted rather than being clamped. (5) max_tokens defaults to 393216, the documented maximum. (6) send() matches, exactly, the seam A1 already wrote into deepseek_transport.py, so that module now reports CLIENT = clients.deepseek_client.

Atria client. Serves stage E's Atria examiner. It keeps the owner's two rules in the file, not in the caller: a lock held across the whole exchange including the streamed read, so only one request is ever in flight; and a ceiling of 65536, the documented maximum, default and parameter, with a gauge - every record carries truncated, true when the finish reason is length - so that if the ceiling was not the cause of the owner's failures it shows. Nothing undocumented is sent (no reasoning_effort, no thinking object), since the service's own page names neither. The same four-value send() shape, so a driver written for one can hold the other.

Mapping to W8: B10 and W3 P4.4 (arm e) get their device; PA.1 gets the request as sent and the reply as returned; A7 and B4 get run-to-run records that can be compared because the raw return is kept; C4 and P4.9 get tool_calls returned whole so a driver can serve the router and record what was opened.

Everything below sends nothing. No key is in the environment (checked: both DEEPSEEK_API_KEY and ATRIA_API_KEY unset), and both clients assert at the end of --dry that their live-attempt counter is zero.

1. python3 deepseek_client.py --dry -> 37 checks passed, 0 failed, "Nothing sent." exit 0.
2. python3 atria_client.py --dry -> 34 checks passed, 0 failed, "Nothing sent." exit 0.
3. python3 deepseek_client.py --dry --save DIR and python3 atria_client.py --dry --save DIR -> six request-text files written to the session scratchpad (plain, prefix, tools; plain, small, tools), each checked to contain no key. The prefix one reads: {"model": "deepseek-flash", "messages": [..., {"role": "assistant", "content": "## 1. The question, frozen\n", "prefix": true}], "max_tokens": 393216, "reasoning_effort": "high", "stream": true, "thinking": {"type": "enabled"}, "stream_options": {"include_usage": true}, "stop": ["\n## 8."]}.
4. The transport paths are driven inside --dry against a stand-in for the requests module that reaches no network: a 200 with a canned SSE stream, a 429 with Retry-After then a 200, a 400 (DeepSeek) and a 401 (Atria), and a non-streamed JSON document. Checked: the reply assembles across chunks including a tool call split over two deltas; a keep-alive comment and blank lines are skipped and the raw lines kept; the retry is recorded as an attempt and not as a second request; the not-retryable status stops at once and keeps its record; the service's words come back unedited; the key is in the header and in no record.
5. Concurrency, with controls. DeepSeek: five jobs at five workers overlap (peak 5), the same five at one worker do not (peak 1). Atria: five threads calling at once are served one at a time (peak 1), and the same run with the lock taken out gives peak 5 - so the check can fail.
6. The seam, for real: from an unrelated working directory, python3 -c importing A1's deepseek_transport gave CLIENT = clients.deepseek_client; then a scratchpad script drove T.send() with T.body_for(prefix=True, max_tokens=32000) through my client with the stubbed transport. It posted to the beta URL, stripped _endpoint from the payload, kept the prefix message intact, sent max_tokens as the caller gave it, and returned the four values A1 unpacks.

predictions_bearing: W10.1 (stage A): the harness dry-runs every arm on one document sending nothing, with the request text saved. Both clients have --dry and --dry --save; the arm (e) prefix shape is among the shapes saved. Falsified by any arm that cannot be dry-run - the prefix shape can be.

W8 PA.1 (compliance count, A1): every run's record carries the number of requests and the text of each request as sent. The client posts the bytes it serialised and returns that text; retries are listed inside the one record so the count PA.1 makes is not inflated by them.

W8 B10 and W3 P4.4 (arm e, the port-setting harness): the test, as W10 section 10 says, is DeepSeek's prefix completion. The client supports it on the beta host with the assistant prefix message the documentation requires.
W10 section 2 (the agents and their limits): five DeepSeek agents at a time through its API. The client will not run more than five worker threads and raises rather than clamping.

W10 addendum, decision W7 (Atria): complex analysis, one request at a time, token ceilings significantly larger. The lock is in the client; the ceiling is the service's maximum and a parameter; truncated is the gauge on that decision.

W3 P4.6 and W8 P4.9 (the modules-opened trace): tool_calls are assembled and returned whole across streamed chunks, so a driver can serve the router and take the trace from the transport's own record rather than the reader's list.
W8 A7 and B4 (a difference read only beyond the run-to-run spread): the raw return is kept as it came, so two repeats can be compared on what the service actually sent, not on a summary of it.
Not served by this deliverable: W10.3 and the fourth clause (A3's task), W10.2 (A2's corpus), W10.4 (the reviewer), and every stage B to F prediction - none of which a client can bear on.

could_not_settle:
Nothing was sent, so nothing here is settled by the service. Every claim about behaviour under load, about what the service accepts, and about what it returns is claimed from documentation or worked out, never seen.

DeepSeek, not settled and named in the file: (1) whether the beta prefix endpoint accepts thinking mode on deepseek-flash - no page found says, and the client does not drop thinking to make a request succeed, because a run under a different thinking setting is a different arm; (2) whether the service refuses a max_tokens that, with the prompt, would overrun the 1M context, which is the thing that would show the 393216 default wrong.

Atria, eight questions, all in the read-me and none answerable from the web: what the owner's failure actually looked like (the client assumes a cut-off reply and gauges it, but a timeout or a 429 would mean the retry schedule or the read timeout is the thing to move); what max_tokens is when omitted; whether the HTTP API takes reasoning_effort or thinking; whether the reply carries a reasoning field and under what name; whether tool calls are accepted on the chat-completions path, which matters if an Atria examiner is ever to open a skill module; whether there is a concurrency limit separate from 60 requests a minute; whether any prefill of the assistant turn exists; and what it costs.

Also unsettled: I read A1's deepseek_transport.py while A1 was still working, so my reading of that seam is of a moving file. And the lock that keeps Atria to one at a time is per-process; two processes would defeat it, and nothing here stops that.
for_the_reviewer:
Press first on the token ceiling. The task for A6 says "no token limit below the service's maximum". I read that as being about the client's own default and not as a veto on a caller's value, so the client defaults to 393216 and sends A1's 32000 unchanged with a stderr note. If the plan meant the stronger reading, the client is wrong and should refuse a low ceiling - but then A1's transport and my client cannot both be right, and one of the two files has to change. Decide it, and note that arm (e) prefills the emission and the port-setting reports are the long ones.

Second, the Atria diagnosis. The owner said it "tends to fail otherwise", and I assumed the failure is truncation and built a ceiling at the maximum plus a truncated gauge. The assumption is a guess dressed in a gauge. If the owner remembers a timeout or a 429 instead, the ceiling is idle and the retry schedule or the read timeout is the part that should have moved. Ask the owner question 1 of the read-me before stage E spends anything.

Third, streaming on by default for Atria. The reason is carried over from the DeepSeek rig's docstring - fitted on another service, untested here. Atria's page says SSE is supported and says nothing about partial output.

Fourth, my checks are my own. I wrote the code, the stand-in and the cases, so a clean sweep proves little; the two things worth weighing are that two of the checks caught real faults (a non-retryable failure threw the request record away, and Retry-After: 0 was falsy and fell through to a four-second backoff), and that the one-at-a-time and five-worker checks now each carry a control that fails. Every other check would pass on a client that never works against the real service.

Fifth, I read A1's deepseek_transport.py while A1 was still writing. Re-check the seam before stage C.
